terms.grammar: verb, first conjugation; with an accusative and infinitive
evidence: Caes. BG 1.39.1: ingentī magnitūdine corporum Germānōs … esse praedicābant
Traupman 147, 291: Praedicat sē reī pūblicae prōfutūrum esse
terms.comment: Of saying out loud, to all and sundry, that something is so; ut praedicās, “as you claim” (Cic. Cat. 1.23, in Lewis & Short). Not praedīcō, praedīcere, foretell.

evidence: Ter. Ph. 743: quem semper tē esse dictitāstī
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: “to declare, maintain, assert repeatedly”; Caesar’s ut dictitābat, “as he claimed”, gives a pretext.

evidence: Cic. Arch. 15: atque īdem ego hoc contendō
terms.comment: With an accusative and infinitive: to argue a point hard.

evidence: Cic. Div. 2.8: nihil ut adfirmem, quaeram omnia

phrases.latin: Quid? nōn, obsecrō, es quem semper tē esse dictitāstī?
phrases.english: What? Aren’t you, if you please, the man you always claimed to be?

sources: Lewis & Short: praedico · Lewis & Short: dictito · Lewis & Short: contendo · Lewis & Short: affirmo
Caes. BG 1.39.1, Ter. Ph. 742b–743, Cic. Arch. 15 and Div. 2.8 checked against the Perseus Latin texts (9 November 2026).
